t:
(a) 
Section 615 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (relating to exploration expenditures) is amended by adding at the end thereof the following new subsections:

“(e) 
Election To Have Section Apply.—This section (other than subsections (f) and (g)) shall apply only if the taxpayer so elects in such manner as the Secretary or his delegate may by regulations prescribe. Such election shall be made before the expiration of 3 years after the time prescribed by law (determined without any extension thereof) for filing the return for the first taxable year ending after the date of the enactment of this subsection in which expenditures described in subsection (a) are paid or incurred after such date. Such election may not be revoked after the expiration of such 3 years.

“(f) 
Section 615 and Section 617 Elections To Be Mutually Exclusive.—A taxpayer who has made an election under subsection (e) (which he has not revoked) may not make an election under section 617(a). A taxpayer who has made an election under section 617 (a) (which he has not revoked) may not make an election under subsection (e) of this section.

“(g) 
Effect of Transfer of Mineral Property.—

“(1) 
Transfer before election.—
If—

“(A) 
any person transfers any mineral property to another person in a transaction as a result of which the basis of such property in the hands of the transferee is determined by reference to the basis in the hands of the transferor, and


“(B) 
the transferor has not, at the time of the transfer, made an election under either subsection (a) of section 617 or subsection (e) of this section,

then no election by the transferor under either such subsection shall apply with respect to expenditures which are made by the transferor after the date of the enactment of this subsection and before the date of the transfer and which are properly chargeable to such property. For purposes of the preceding sentence, a transferor or mineral property who made an election under subsection (a) of section 617 or subsection (e) of this section before the transfer but who revokes such election after the transfer shall lie treated with respect to such property as not having made an election under either such subsection.


“(2) 
Effect of election by transferee under section 617.—
If—

“(A) 
the taxpayer receives mineral property in a transaction described in paragraph (1)(A),


“(B) 
an election made by the transferor under subsection (e) applies with respect to expenditures which are made by him after the date of the enactment of this subsection and before the date of the transfer and which are properly chargeable to such property, and


“(C) 
the taxpayer has made or makes an election under section 617(a),

then in applying section 617 with respect to the transferee, the amounts allowed as deduct ions under this section to the transferor, which (but for the transferor’s election) would lie reflected in the adjusted basis of such property in the hands of the transferee, shall be treated as expenditures allowed as deductions under section 617(a) to the transferor. Notwithstanding subsections (b) and (d) of this section (and section 381(c)(10)), any deferred expenses described in subsection (b) which are not allowed as deductions to the transferor for a period before the transfer may not be deducted by the transferee and in his hands shall be charged to capital account.”




 
    (b) Section 7034b) of such Code (relating to elections of partnerships) is amended by inserting after “United States,” the following: “and any election under section 615 (relating to exploration expenditures) or under section 617 (relating to additional exploration expenditures in the case of domestic mining),”.

fable.w: The section authorizes the Secretary or his delegate to prescribe regulations governing how the election is made, and a grant of rulemaking authority counts as participation under the definition, even when phrased with "may" (as in the worked example on regulatory authority). The tempting reading is that this is only a tax provision about private taxpayer elections, which on their own are not participation in a federal decision. That reading overlooks the rulemaking authority, which is the only basis for the Yes label.
fable.s: This section (other than subsections (f) and (g)) shall apply only if the taxpayer so elects in such manner as the Secretary or his delegate may by regulations prescribe.

qwen_block.w: This section outlines tax code provisions regarding elections made by taxpayers for exploration expenditures. The 'election' is a unilateral action by the taxpayer, not a participatory process involving consultation with the government. While the Secretary may prescribe regulations, the text does not mandate a specific participatory mechanism (like a public comment period or advisory board) for those regulations, nor does it involve the government consulting with outsiders before a decision. Tax elections are analogous to applications, which are excluded from the definition of participation.
qwen_block.s: This section (other than subsections (f) and (g)) shall apply only if the taxpayer so elects in such manner as the Secretary or his delegate may by regulations prescribe.
qwen_block.b:
Temptation: The text mentions that the Secretary may prescribe regulations for how an election is made. One might think that rulemaking inherently involves public participation (comment periods, etc.). However, the section itself does not mandate a specific participatory process (like a hearing or comment period); it merely grants the authority to issue regulations. More importantly, the core of the section is about tax elections by private taxpayers, which are applications/declarations, not participation in government decision-making. The definition explicitly excludes applications for benefits or grants, and tax elections are analogous in that they are unilateral actions by the taxpayer to determine their tax liability, not a consultation with the government.

Resolution: The section describes tax code amendments regarding elections for exploration expenditures. It does not require the government to consult with outsiders before making a decision. The "election" is made by the taxpayer, not the government. The Secretary's role is to prescribe regulations, but the text does not describe a participatory process for those regulations. Therefore, it is "No".

opus.w: The section lets the Secretary of the Treasury set the manner of the election by regulation. Under the definition and Example 6, authorizing agency rulemaking counts as participation because it brings in the public notice-and-comment process. The tempting 'No' reading treats this as a mere taxpayer election, but the regulation grant alone meets the 'requiring rulemaking' test, even though the rest of the section is technical tax mechanics.
opus.s: This section (other than subsections (f) and (g)) shall apply only if the taxpayer so elects in such manner as the Secretary or his delegate may by regulations prescribe.
opus.b: The tempting reading is "No": this section is mostly about how a taxpayer makes, and is bound by, a tax election, which is a private filing choice rather than outsiders taking part in a federal decision. That reading fails because the definition counts "requiring rulemaking" as participation. Example 6 treats any grant of authority for an agency to issue regulations as participation, even when the agency has discretion ("may"). Here the Secretary prescribes by regulation how the election is made, so the section authorizes rulemaking.

qwen_chat.w: This section deals with tax elections and the transfer of mineral property between private parties. While it mentions that the Secretary may prescribe regulations for how an election is made, it does not require consultation with outside parties, public hearings, or advisory committees with non-federal members. The regulatory authority is procedural and internal to the agency's administration of the tax code, not a participatory process involving the public or other outside entities in the decision-making itself.
qwen_chat.s: This section (other than subsections (f) and (g)) shall apply only if the taxpayer so elects in such manner as the Secretary or his delegate may by regulations prescribe.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the phrase "in such manner as the Secretary or his delegate may by regulations prescribe" implies a rulemaking process, which often involves public comment periods (participation). However, the definition explicitly states that "requiring rulemaking" is a form of participation, but this section merely grants the *authority* to prescribe regulations for an election procedure. More importantly, the core of the section is about tax elections and transfers of property between private parties. There is no requirement for the Secretary to consult with outsiders, hold hearings, or form advisory committees with non-federal members. The "regulations" mentioned are procedural rules for filing tax elections, not substantive policy decisions requiring external input. The section does not mandate any interaction with the public, states, or other outside entities before a decision is made. It is purely an internal administrative mechanism for tax code implementation.
